{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=quantitative+benchmarks+and+metrics+for+evaluating+autonomous+scientific+problem+formulation+and+agenda+setting&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.36227/techrxiv.177162480.04513202/v2\", \"title\": [\"Evaluating Agentic Artificial Intelligence: A Comprehensive Survey of Metrics, Benchmarks, and Methodologies\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI) refers to autonomous systems capable of multi-step planning, subgoal generation, tool use, adaptation, and sustained decisionmaking. As such systems are increasingly deployed in robotics, scientific discovery, software engineering, and large language model (LLM)-based agents, the need for rigorous and multidimensional evaluation has become critical. However, existing evaluation practices, largely inherited from supervised learning and short-horizon reinforcement learning, fail to capture essential agentic properties such as long-horizon coherence, robustness under uncertainty, autonomy, safety, and adaptive behavior. This survey presents a structured and comprehensive analysis of evaluation methodologies for Agentic AI. We introduce an elevendimensional taxonomy encompassing task success, output quality, planning and reasoning, decision-making under uncertainty, tooluse effectiveness, autonomy and human intervention, learning and adaptation, safety and alignment, efficiency and resource utilization, multi-agent collaboration, and long-term memory consistency. Using this taxonomy, we systematically examine the growing ecosystem of benchmarks, frameworks, and evaluation tools, highlighting how they assess agent interactions, behavioral trajectories, and long-horizon performance across reinforcement learning agents, LLM-based agents, and multi-agent systems. Building on this analysis, we identify persistent evaluation gaps, including non-determinism, limited reproducibility, benchmark overfitting, incomplete safety assessment, and insufficient longhorizon evaluation. We conclude by outlining future research directions toward standardized, interpretable, and reliabilityfocused evaluation frameworks that more accurately reflect the real-world capabilities, limitations, and risks of Agentic AI.</jats:p>\",…

CVEVOLVE: ZERO-CODEAUTONOMOUSALGORITHM
DISCOVERY FORUNSTRUCTUREDSCIENTIFICDATA
PROCESSING
Ming Du∗, Xiangyu Yin, Yanqi Luo, Dishant Beniwal, Songyuan Tang, Hemant Sharma, Mathew J. Cherukara†
Advanced Photon Source
Argonne National Laboratory
Lemont, IL, USA
∗mingdu@anl.gov,†mcherukara@anl.gov
ABSTRACT
Scientific data processing often requires task-specific algorithms or AI models, creating a barrier
for domain scientists who need to analyze their data but may not have extensive computing or
image-processing expertise. This barrier is especially pronounced when data are noisy, have a
high dynamic range, are sparsely labeled, or are only loosely specified. We introduce CVEvolve,
an autonomous agentic harness with a zero-code interface for scientific data-processing algorithm
discovery. CVEvolve combines a multi-round search strategy with tools for code execution, evaluation
implementation, history management, holdout testing, and optional inspection of scientific data and
visual outputs. The search alternates between discovery and improvement actions, and uses lineage-
aware stochastic candidate sampling to balance exploration and exploitation. We demonstrate
CVEvolve on X-ray fluorescence microscopy image registration, Bragg peak detection, high-energy
diffraction microscopy image segmentation, and hybrid analytical–learning-based affine registration.

Autonomous robots operating in open and changing environments must adapt not only what they know, but also how they think, learn, and interact when previously unseen situations arise. However, most existing approaches assume predefined reasoning, learning, or interaction mechanisms and mainly adapt knowledge or model parameters within these fixed structures. This paper proposes an open-ended cognitive evolution framework that maintains a minimal cognitive core while allowing concrete thinking, learning, and interaction methods to be selected, validated, reused, updated, and expanded according to observed evidence and accumulated experience. The framework also incorporates discrepancy-driven evaluation to detect when previously valid knowledge or capabilities have become outdated. Experiments over five independent seeds show that newly acquired thinking activities achieve 94.67% first-encounter success on unseen conflict families, with 98.67% reuse. Adaptive learning-method selection reaches 95.00% accuracy and improves task success to 69.16%, compared with 55.66% for the best fixed learner. Under unannounced environmental changes, the proposed method achieves 96.43% task success, only 1.07% hazard rate and 1.43% outdated decisions, while reducing verification operations by 48.0% relative to periodic updating.
